Strategic HR

Say it early.

A teacher who names the problem early, with one fact and one request, is easier to keep. The same skill works with a coordinator and with a parent.

Talk about these first

Then read the article and see who agrees with you.

  1. Think of a teacher who changed something for you. What did they do?
    “My English teacher never laughed when I made a mistake. She waited, and she let me finish the sentence. I think that is why I kept speaking.”
  2. What is the hardest part of a teacher’s day, in your opinion?
    “I think it is everything around the class: marking, meetings, messages from parents. The lesson itself is the easy part.”
  3. Is it harder to be a teacher today than twenty years ago? Why?
    “I think so. Teachers now deal with phones, large groups and parents who write at any hour. The job has grown, but the day has not.”
  4. A friend who teaches says she is exhausted. What do you say? What do you not say?
    “I would say, “That sounds heavy. What is taking most of your energy?” I would not say, “Just rest more,” because it sounds like it is her fault.”
  5. Should a school ask its teachers why they stay, or wait until they resign?
    “It should ask. Waiting until someone resigns is too late. A short, regular conversation costs almost nothing.”
Society · Education

Why are teachers leaving the classroom?

The world needs 44 million more teachers by 2030. Most of those jobs are not new. They are replacements.

By EIC Magazine · 4 min read · Hover over the dotted words to see them in Portuguese

Listen to the article0:00
Speed
The recording is not on this page yet.

In 2024, UNESCO counted how many teachers the world’s schools will need by 2030: 44 million more. The surprise is where most of them are needed. About 58% would replace teachers who leave the profession. Only 42% are new jobs.

A leaking bucket

Between 2015 and 2022, attrition among primary teachers almost doubled, from 4.6% to 9%. In half of all countries, primary teachers are paid less than other professions that need similar qualifications. In the United States, a 2025 RAND survey found that teachers worked 49 hours a week on average, ten more than their contracted hours, and 53% reported burnout. That is a heavy workload.

Satisfied, but not valued

Brazil shows another side. In the OECD’s TALIS 2024 survey, 87% of Brazilian teachers said they were satisfied with their job, close to the OECD average of 89%. But they lose 21% of class time keeping order (the OECD average is 15%), and only 14% believe teachers are valued by society (the average is 22%).

Pay, workload or respect?

Supporters of higher pay say the numbers are clear: people leave when a job pays less than others with the same training. American teachers earn about $73,000 on average, while similar workers earn about $103,000.

Others say the problem is workload and respect. A teacher who loses a fifth of every class to discipline, and who works ten hours beyond the contract, needs support before anything else.

A third group says money is only part of the story. In the United States, the share of teachers who intended to leave fell from 22% to 16% in one year, while the share who said their pay was adequate stayed about the same.

Researcher Ashley Woo warns that “not everyone who says that they are likely to leave is actually going to leave.” But on one point, all sides agree: a school learns more by asking teachers before they leave than after.

“Not everyone who says that they are likely to leave is actually going to leave.”Ashley Woo, researcher, quoted by Education Week

44 millionmore teachers needed worldwide by 2030 (UNESCO, 2024)
58%of them would replace teachers who leave
87% / 14%of Brazilian teachers are satisfied with the job / believe teachers are valued by society (TALIS 2024)
21%of class time lost to keeping order in Brazil. The OECD average is 15%

Sources: UNESCO, Global Report on Teachers (2024); RAND, State of the American Teacher Survey (2025); OECD, TALIS 2024, released 6 October 2025, as reported by Agência Brasil; Education Week (July 2025).

7The ask

Ask in five moves

Name the problem. Give one fact. Ask for one change, and put a date on it.

  1. 1Ask for a meeting

    Could we schedule 20 minutes to talk about my workload?

    Do not start in the corridor.

  2. 2Give one fact

    Here is what I’m seeing: I’m regularly working beyond my contracted hours, mostly on marking and planning.

    One fact first, feeling second.

  3. 3Name the effect

    It’s starting to affect my planning and my energy in class.

    Say the effect on the students, not only on you.

  4. 4Ask for one change

    What I’d like to propose is fewer extra duties until the end of term.

    One request, small enough to say yes to.

  5. 5Put a date on it

    Could we check in again on the 15th?

    A date turns a complaint into a plan.

Too blunt, say this

Say the better version out loud first. Then tap to check.

I can’t take this anymore.I’m at my limit with the current workload. Could we look at options?
You give us too much work.Could we review my workload and see what can come off my plate?
Nobody listens to teachers here.Could I share some feedback from the classroom?
I’m thinking of quitting.I want to be open with you: I’m not sure this role is sustainable for me. What could change?
That class is out of control.Behaviour is taking a lot of class time. Could we agree on a plan and some support?

With a parent: hard news in three moves

Describe the behaviour, not the child. “He hasn’t handed in homework” is something you saw. “He is lazy” is a judgement.

  1. 1Say what you saw.

    “I’ve noticed that Pedro hasn’t handed in his homework for three weeks.”

  2. 2Ask what they see.

    “Does that match what you see at home?”

  3. 3Agree a next step, with a date.

    “Could we try a homework planner and talk again in two weeks?”

8The answer

When the answer is not yet yes

Do not argue. Accept it, ask for something smaller, and put a date on the next talk.

  1. 1Accept it, then ask for something smaller.

    “I understand there is no budget for that. Is there something smaller we could try?”

    A concrete answer (“we can cut one duty in March”) is a real offer. A vague answer is often a soft no.

  2. 2Ask to talk again, with a date.

    “Could we revisit this after the mid-year break?”

  3. 3Ask what would change the answer.

    “What would you need to see from me to make that possible?”

  4. 4When there is another offer, separate the two.

    “That helps, but it doesn’t solve the hours. Could we do both?”

  5. 5When you need time, give a day.

    “Let me think about it and get back to you by Friday.”

A real exchange

Coordinator

Is this about the extra classes, or something bigger?

Teacher

Both. I’m happy to cover them, but I’m regularly working beyond my hours. Could we look at what can come off my plate?

Coordinator

Isn’t everyone busy right now?

Teacher

I hear you. That’s why I’m raising it early, before it affects my classes. Could we check in on the 15th?

When a parent pushes back

Parent

My son is not lazy. I think you just don’t like him.

Teacher

I hear you, and I’m glad you told me. I want him to do well. Could we look at his last three assignments together and agree on one thing to try this month?

Your turn · coordinator

The coordinator says: “We can’t reduce anyone’s hours this term.” Answer in three moves: accept, ask, date.

“Understood, thanks for telling me. Is there a smaller change we could try, like moving one extra duty to someone else? Could we talk again on the 15th, once I’ve sent you a short list?”
Your turn · parent

A parent says: “Other kids talk in class too. Why is it always my daughter?” Answer in three moves: say what you saw, ask, agree a next step.

“It’s a fair question. In the last two weeks I noticed her talking during group work, and I want to understand why. What have you noticed at home? Could we try a seat change and check in again on Friday?”
9Other side

How the school reads it

A coordinator or a head of school does not look at one teacher. She looks at numbers. Here are the numbers and the words she uses.

Satisfied, not valued

All figures in %. OECD, TALIS 2024 (released 6 October 2025), as reported by Agência Brasil.

Numbers you can quote

  • 44 million more teachers are needed worldwide by 2030, and 58% of them would replace teachers who leave. UNESCO, 2024.
  • Attrition among primary teachers almost doubled: 4.6% in 2015, 9% in 2022. UNESCO, 2024.
  • In half of all countries, primary teachers are paid less than other professions that need similar qualifications. UNESCO, 2024.
  • USA, 2025: 53% of teachers report burnout. They work 49 hours a week, ten more than contracted. RAND.

Six terms and the sentence for the meeting

TermIn the meeting
turnover n.“What is our turnover this year, and who is leaving?”
attrition n.“Global attrition among primary teachers almost doubled between 2015 and 2022.”
retain v.“How do we retain our best teachers?” “Retention is a pay question and a workload question.”
workload n.“The current workload is not sustainable.”
backfill v.“We need to backfill two positions before March.”
onboarding n.“Onboarding should include a mentor in the first year.”

A tool for HR: the stay interview

  1. 1What pulls them in

    What do you look forward to each day when you commute to work?

  2. 2Learning

    What are you learning here, and what do you want to learn?

  3. 3Why they stay

    Why do you stay here?

  4. 4Thinking of leaving

    When is the last time you thought about leaving us, and what prompted it?

  5. 5What you can do

    What can I do to make your job better for you?

Source: Richard Finnegan, SHRM. Ask every employee the same questions and listen 80% of the time. A stay interview asks people who are still here. An exit interview asks people who are leaving.

Your turn · stay interview

Choose two of the five questions and ask a colleague. Listen 80% of the time. Then say back what you heard in one sentence.

“So the thing you look forward to is the students, and the thing that almost made you leave was the amount of marking. Did I get that right?”

11Glossary

Watch out, then look it up

False friends

WordFrom the PortugueseWhat it really means
parentsparentesIt means mother and father. For aunts, uncles and cousins, say relatives.
attritionatritoIt means people leaving over time. For friction between people, say friction.
collegecolégioIt means a school at university level. For a school for children, say school.
supportsuportarIt means to help. For “I can’t stand this,” say I can’t cope with it.
pretendpretenderIt means to act as if. For to plan, say intend or plan.
retireretirarIt means to stop working because of age. For to take back, say withdraw.
